An MLP neural network is trained to predict the stress-strain curve of additively manufactured parts based on metal properties and fabrication methods used. The MLP model performs reasonably well in some cases (like in (a)) but shows significant discrepancies in others. This suggests that while the model can capture the general trend of stress-strain relationships, it may struggle with certain material conditions or specific specimens. These differences could be due to variations in the specimens that the model wasn't fully trained on, highlighting the need for further tuning, more representative training data, or possibly a more complex model. Exploring more advanced models, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformer-based architectures, might help address the issues with variability and improve the model’s robustness. Some of the observations and results were discussed with the stakeholders, whose insights were invaluable. Figure 42 illustrates six example specimens that exhibit varying stress-strain curves, despite being produced by the same manufacturer and using identical build parameters. The stakeholders acknowledged that such variations in maximum force/stress experienced and the distance traveled before catastrophic failure (breakage at the end of the test) are anticipated. They also identified that the stress-strain curve for Specimen 1 likely reflects a data collection issue. Additionally, while Specimens 2, 4, and 6 display a sudden fracture at the end of the test, with the material clearly breaking into two, Specimen 3 demonstrates the gradual decline characteristic of a highly ductile material that stretches steadily until failure. Specimen 5 shows a pattern where the material partially breaks, then stretches, and repeats this process before ultimately failing. The stakeholders also decided to uniformly trim the tails of the curves across all samples to ensure consistent data processing for each specimen. An updated dataset is received.
